paras: The attempted lynching of Morgan Richards took place near Gore, Hocking County, Ohio, on December 29, 1881, when a mob tried to take Richards, a farm hand accused of murdering his aunt, from the officers who had arrested him. The officers repulsed the mob and lodged him in the jail at Logan. Wire reports carried the story nationally as a crime item, and several predicted that he would still be lynched.

At about 6:30 on the evening of December 28, an unknown man opened the door of the house of Mrs. Terrell, a widow living on the outskirts of Gore, and shot her dead in front of her two grown daughters. Her son William was serving a life term in the Ohio Penitentiary for the triple murder of the Weldon family near Gore. The New-York Tribune's first report said there was no clue to the killer and that "vigilance committees" were scouring the country, and a Kentucky paper called them "lynching committees".

Authorities guarded the house overnight to preserve the killer's tracks, and at daylight they followed them to the farm of a man named Arnold, where they arrested Morgan Richards, one of his farm hands. Richards carried a revolver with one empty chamber and resisted arrest before he was overpowered and put in a wagon.

Accounts of what followed differ in detail. According to a Cincinnati special, the wagon was driven rapidly to Logan jail, "barely escaping a lynching party" that tried to head it off. A separate Gore dispatch said a mob tried to take Richards from the officers and was repulsed, and one version added that the mob carried ropes and meant to hang him to a nearby tree before the sheriff got him into jail.

A dispatch to the Cincinnati Commercial reported that Richards had confessed to killing Mrs. Terrell, his mother's sister, over "an old grudge". The same dispatch offered two theories, that he killed her to keep her from revealing others implicated in her son's crime and that he sought notoriety after following the Guiteau trial, and it reported "still talk of lynching him". Another account had Richards claiming to know who had planned the Weldon murders.
Briefs a week later reported only that Richards had been arrested and charged with the murder, and the coverage includes no report of a further lynching attempt, an inquest, an indictment or a trial.

White papers from Maine to Texas ran the story on December 30 and 31, mostly as two Cincinnati wire dispatches, one on the arrest and one on the confession, under crime headings such as "Arrest of the Assassin of Mrs. Terrell", "A Causeless Crime" and "Emulating Guiteau". The Morning Journal and Courier headed its version "A Brute in Danger of Lynching" and predicted he would "no doubt be lynched", and the daily gazette called it the "Murder of an Old Lady by a Farm Hand" and said no doubt existed that he would be. No paper condemned the mob, and none mentioned the race of anyone involved.
Reprints continued into January, including the Somerset Herald's "Narrow Escape from Lynchin[g]", while the Ohio and Missouri weekly summaries dropped the mob altogether.

bases: A mob tried to take a murder suspect from officers to hang him and was repulsed, an attempted lynching (A2, A3, A14); no paper gives the race of anyone involved.

A mob acting on the murder accusation tried to seize and hang Richards but was repulsed and he was jailed, so no one was killed (A3, A14); this is an attempted lynching, and nothing in the coverage shows a racial dimension.
Two differently worded Gore dispatches, the Cincinnati special (A2, A5) and the dispatch printed in A3 and A14, both report a lynching party or mob that failed to take Richards from the officers.
